The Andean long-clawed mouse (Chelemys macronyx) is a cricetid rodent inhabiting the temperate forests and high-altitude grasslands of southern South America, where its life history traits reflect the challenges of a cold, seasonal environment. Reproductive output in this species is modest but consistent with that of other small mammals occupying similar niches. Females typically produce litters of six to seven pups [N_R_i = litters of six to seven pups], and under optimal thermal conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], they may sustain approximately four litters per year [F_R_i = approximately four litters per year], resulting in a maximum reproductive rate that has been quantified in laboratory colonies. This relatively low fecundity per event is balanced by what appears to be a stable, year-round breeding strategy, though most parturition events are concentrated during the austral spring and summer months, when resource availability peaks. The gestation period required to bring a litter to term is eighteen days [tg = eighteen days] when measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that places Chelemys macronyx among the more rapidly developing cricetids, a trait likely advantageous for completing multiple breeding attempts within a single favorable season.

Neonatal development in Chelemys macronyx follows an altricial pattern typical of many murid rodents, with the newborn completely dependent on maternal care during the first weeks of life. At parturition, each pup weighs approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], a remarkably small birth mass that underscores the limited energetic investment per offspring at the moment of delivery. This modest initial mass belies a relatively rapid growth trajectory, and the species shares with related sigmodontines the challenge of converting maternal milk into somatic tissue quickly enough to reduce vulnerability to predation and thermal stress. The high surface-area-to-volume ratio of these tiny neonates places them at significant risk of hypothermia, a constraint that likely explains the species' reliance on well-insulated subterranean nest chambers. Lactation constitutes the primary energetic bottleneck of reproduction for the female, who must sustain a substantial increase in milk synthesis to support the growing litter. Under captive conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the complete period of nutritional dependence from birth to nutritional independence has been carefully documented.

Weaning represents a critical transition in the life cycle of the Andean long-clawed mouse, marking the point at which the young begin to forage independently and the mother's reproductive investment in that particular litter effectively ceases. Observations of captive colonies indicate that pups are fully weaned and capable of surviving on solid food alone at twenty days after birth [tx = twenty days after birth], with this milestone measured under the standard thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This weaning age is relatively brief compared to some other cricetids of similar body size, perhaps reflecting the species' need to compress the period of parental dependency within a short favorable season. After weaning, the juvenile enters a period of rapid somatic growth during which it must acquire the body mass and physiological competence required for eventual reproduction. The energetic demands of this sub-adult phase are considerable, and individuals allocate most of their assimilated energy toward increasing structural size and building lipid reserves that will support future reproductive effort. The timing of subsequent developmental milestones is closely tied to the prevailing thermal environment.

Sexual maturation in Chelemys macronyx occurs after a predictable interval following birth, defining the age at which individuals become capable of contributing to the next generation. Under the consistent temperature conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] in controlled laboratory settings, the time since birth at puberty is twenty-six days (26 days since birth) [tp = 26 days since birth], a relatively rapid maturation schedule that allows young born early in the breeding season to potentially reproduce within the same calendar year. This abbreviated interval to reproductive competence is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy adapted to environments where the window for successful breeding may be unpredictable or constrained by harsh winter conditions. Once pubertal, both males and females exhibit fully developed gonadal function, and mating behavior can be observed shortly thereafter. The attainment of adult body mass typically follows puberty rather than preceding it, meaning that many young females undergo their first ovulation while still below the species' ultimate body weight. This decoupling of somatic growth from reproductive maturation is not uncommon among small rodents.

The ultimate adult body mass achieved by Chelemys macronyx in the wild is approximately 62 grams [Wwi = approximately 62 grams], a figure derived from extensive trapping surveys and museum specimen collections across the species' range. This body size places it among the medium-to-large members of its genus and reflects the energetic demands of both thermoregulation and activity in a cool, mesic environment. Basal metabolic rate has been assessed using flow-through respirometry, with the maximum recorded resting oxygen consumption reaching 84.32 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 84.32 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animals were maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively elevated metabolic rate is consistent with the species' active, fossorial lifestyle and its occupancy of cold habitats where maintaining endothermy is energetically costly. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 5.3 years [am = approximately 5.3 years], as reconstructed from mark-recapture studies conducted at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] in captive reference conditions, though field mortality rates suggest that very few individuals reach this extreme age.

The Andean long-clawed mouse occupies a range of elevations stretching from lowland Nothofagus forests to high-altitude puna grasslands, habitats that impose contrasting selective pressures on its physiology and behavior. Field surveys across the Patagonian region have noted that burrow systems often incorporate an extensive network of tunnels and multiple nesting chambers, likely serving both thermal insulation and predator avoidance functions. These subterranean refuges buffer against the extreme daily temperature fluctuations typical of the arid and semi-arid zones within its distribution, permitting a relatively stable body temperature even when ambient conditions vary widely. The species' capacity for sustained metabolic activity under such conditions is reflected in its relatively high basal oxygen consumption, which supports not only routine maintenance but also the energetic demands of digging, foraging, and territorial defense. Predation pressure from raptors, canids, and snakes may further limit population densities and influence the timing of reproductive events across the annual cycle.
